newsitem.title: USA: IFC - private development financing growth slowing.
newsitem.headline: IFC - private development financing growth slowing.

text.p: The International Finance Corporation Thursday said strong developing country financing growth continued last year but the pace will moderate slightly as others help take up the cause of private development.
The World Bank affiliate that helps private enterprise in the developing world said total financing in the year to June 30 hit a record $3.2 billion against $2.9 in fiscal 1995.
At a briefing to unveil its annual report, IFC Executive Vice President Jannik Lindbaek told reporters he expected total financing this year would be up eight to 10 percent.

Lindbaek said this was somewhat slower than in recent years, noting that over the past five years total financing by the agency has doubled as countries around the world rushed to embrace the free enterprise system.

"We see that in some of our important countries, alternative sources of financing have become available, so we are less important to some of (them)," he said, adding: "we're talking about Eastern Europe and some parts of Asia."

At the same time, he said the IFC was launching an initiative to expand its activities in smaller and poorer nations, targeting some 16 countries it said were undergoing particularly difficult transitions to market economies.
They included Bosnia and Herzegovina, Cambodia, countries in the Eastern Caribbean, Central Africa, as well as the Slovak Republic and the West Bank and Gaza.
"We are devoting increased resources to small and medium-sized enterprises," Lindbaek said, adding: "We continue to pioneer in new sectors and countries."
The IFC also said it is working hard to ensure it does not get in the way of private capital moving into developing markets by extensive consultation with the private sector.
The IFC said its focus remained on meeting the needs for building private infrastructure, such as roads and bridges, as well as supporting private capital market development.
In its catalyst role, it said syndications with financial institutions last year reached $4.8 billion, a staggering 88 percent increase over 1995.
The increase, including loans, equity deals and syndications, was 47 percent higher than 1995.
It approved projects in 68 countries last year, including some 71 for sub Saharan Africa, the largest for any region.
